newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Thousands protest Serbian local election results.
newsitem.headline: Thousands protest Serbian local election results.

text.p: Leaders of Serbia's opposition coalition Zajedno met Western diplomats on Monday, as about thousands of opponents of the government's annulment of election results staged Belgrade's biggest demonstration since 1991.

European Union officials and ambassadors from 13 western embassies talked with Zajedno (Together) leaders after a similar meeting with the Yugoslav foreign minister Milan Milutinovic over the weekend.

As the talks ended, a crowd estimated by journalists at 200,000 tossed eggs at the state-controlled Radio and Television building and the offices of the Politika newspaper, targeting two of president Slobodan Milosevic's key instruments of power.
The peaceful protesters jeered at the buildings and chanted anti-communist slogans such as "Red Gang" and "Out, Out".
Independent radio B-92 said the crowd filled the street from the Serbian Parliament building to the Republic Square some 1.5 kilometres (one mile) away and was continuing to grow.
"These are not elections between parties," declared one speaker. "These are elections between democracy and darkness."

The protest came a day after the state-controlled electoral commission in Belgrade took back 33 local council seats won by Zajedno, citing unspecified irregularites, and called for a third round of voting on Wednesday.
The state news agency Tanjug declared that a campaign blackout began at midnight on Sunday, in a tactic analysts say was designed to stifle the protests ahead of the polls.

After polling eight days ago, the Socialists at first conceded they had lost councils in industrial towns across Serbia including Belgrade, but electoral commissions later annulled the results in almost all the districts Zajedno won.
Zajedno has urged a boycott of the third round of voting in the capital and other key towns where they say they were cheated of legal victories.
Although diplomatic sources confirmed that the ambassadors' meetings with both Milutinovic and Zajedno discussed the growing crisis, they maintained a disciplined silence over the diplomats' message.
One Western source who declined to be named said Zajedno outlined the legal steps they planned to use to challenge the Socialists' tactics.
But a Zajedno statement issued after the talks declared the decision to cancel results is "the greatest nullification of elections since Yugoslavia was created in 1918".

"(The Socialist's) political and legal strategy is aimed at exhausting and manipulating the electorate, as well as provoking protests of citizens which could be a reason for declearing a state of emergency," the statement said.

The opposition Democratic Party's foreign affairs spokesman Ilija Djukic who met the diplomats said states enforcing the Dayton peace agreement for Bosnia which Milosevic signed should also force him to respect other democratic conventions.
"These are the reasons Zajedno is calling for civil disobedience, and why it is using all legal and legitimate means to defend its victory," he said.
Western countries have expressed dismay at the way Milosevic's ruling Socialist Party handled the elections which gave an unexpected victory to Zajedno in most major towns.
But they have so far offered only muted statements of concern over possible election fraud.
The United States and European powers once accused Milosevic of igniting war in the former Yugoslavia.

They now view him as a guarantor of Balkan peace after he signed the U.S.- brokered peace treaty last year and may wish to avoid an open confrontation. But western states still have indirect weapons available.

These include adding fairness in elections to existing conditions - such as a peaceful solution to an ethnic dispute in Kosovo and compliance with the Bosnia peace process - as the price for normalising international relations with Yugoslavia.
But Djukic insisted the Western view was misplaced.
"Milosevic is not the only guarantor of stability in this region," he told Reuters.
